disclosures.name: TestCaller
disclosures.reason: runtime-capability: symtab_test.go's assertion requires f.Entry() < pc -- the function's entry address always strictly precedes a call site's return address within it. go2cs has no addresses, only opaque per-call-site PC tokens (the deliberate model managed_impl.cs's header documents throughout); FuncForPC(pc) mints a *Func whose Entry() returns that SAME token, so Entry() == pc by construction and the < assertion can never hold. Inventing a value strictly less than the token (e.g. subtracting a constant) would satisfy the assert with a number that means nothing this host can stand behind -- the same class of laundering the ManagedPointerTokens/reflect pointer-identity disclosures already refuse. Falsifiable in the parts that matter: the same assertion also checks ok, Name()'s suffix, and the file/line range: if any of THOSE ever mismatch, the row is a real defect, not this disclosure -- only the Entry()>=pc arm is pinned. Measured 2026-09-02: ok=true, Name()=the correct qualified name, file/line correct, Entry()==pc exactly (e.g. 27==27) on every reported iteration.

disclosures.name: TestFunctionAlignmentTraceback
disclosures.signature: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
disclosures.reason: runtime-capability: the test reads the CODE BYTE at a PC, *(*uint8)(unsafe.Pointer(pc)) at symtab_test.go:240, one byte before a caller token, expecting the INT3 alignment filler (0xcc) that the Go linker pads functions with. go2cs has no machine code at a PC: runtime.Caller answers an opaque call-site token from a non-canonical band (runtime/managed_impl.cs s_callerSpanBase, 0x8000_8000_0000_0000, TRAIN C's caller-PC spans 96ce90f997), so no byte exists there to read. The read is refused by golib's minted-address sink guard (ManagedPointerTokens.NamesNoUserMemory, bit 63) as Go's nil-dereference panic on EVERY platform. Before that guard the same read was a caught NullReferenceException on linux, because a non-canonical #GP reports address 0 there, and a FATAL AccessViolation on windows that ended the test host at test F and blanked every later verdict of the row (measured 2026-09-27: bisected to ed9dc138e8, pc = 0x800080000000F7FF printed at the site). Pinned to that panic text on this test alone: any OTHER failure here (the FuncForPC name check, or Frames.Next's Func) is a real defect, not this disclosure.

disclosures.name: TestPinnerConstStringData
disclosures.reason: runtime-capability: the test's own comment states its subject -- 'const string data is not in span'. It asserts that unsafe.StringData of a string LITERAL reads runtime.isPinned == true before, during and after a Pinner.Pin/Unpin, which is true in Go because RODATA is not a heap span: spanOfHeap answers nil and the non-Go-pointer arm answers pinned. golib has no RODATA -- a literal's bytes are a heap byte[] (rooted for the process's life but movable) and unsafe.StringData returns an element reference into it -- so the truthful managed answer for that storage is 'a Go heap object, not pinned', and that is what the row reads on its FIRST assertion, before Pin is ever called. Answering true for storage nothing pinned would be fabrication (this class's anti-laundering clause). A truthful form exists in principle -- literal storage on the Pinned Object Heap plus a registry of literal-backed arrays so isPinned can recognise them -- and is REFUSED as one row's consumer paying a corpus-wide, unpriced allocation-policy change; that form is this entry's rejoin clause. Only the first-assertion arm is pinned: Pin and Unpin on that pointer must still not panic, so a regression in the non-Go-pointer no-op reads as a defect, not as this disclosure. Design and prediction: docs/phase4/DESIGN-runtime-pinner.md section 6.1.

disclosures.name: TestPanicSystemstack
disclosures.reason: host-fatal HANG member (the class was widened to admit a deadline-consuming hang beside a crash, coordinator ruling 2026-09-05, recorded at hostFatalClass in testConversion.go; this row RATIFIED as a member by coordinator ruling 2026-09-05 over C1's Q46 reading). The test re-execs the host with the argument testPanicSystemstackInternal; the child's crash_unix_test.go init() starts one goroutine and then calls testPanicSystemstackInternal on the initializing thread, each meant to print "x\n" and then deadlock on a runtime lock inside systemstack so that a SIGQUIT under GOTRACEBACK=crash prints both blocked stacks. MEASURED (solo, Release+TC0, 3 m deadline; Go=pass): the converted child prints ONE x, because the goroutine started inside init() cannot enter testPanicSystemstackInternal until the CLR type-initializer lock is released by the module initializer it was started from -- and that initializer is deadlocking itself by the test's own design (dotnet-stack: main thread = <Module>..cctor -> initΔ3 -> lock2 spinning; goroutine = Goroutine.Run with no body frame, its thread in a futex wait). Go runs init-started goroutines concurrently with init; the CLR serializes every other thread's first touch of an initializing type behind its constructor. The parent therefore never completes io.ReadFull(pr, 4), never sends SIGQUIT, never reaches its deferred Process.Kill, and consumes the package deadline; the deadline's external SIGKILL orphans a child that a hand-sent SIGQUIT kills at once (its SIGQUIT is unblocked and caught, SigPnd empty). NOT a missing feature: the class censused in the pinned GOROOT (a go statement lexically inside func init()) is 2 production + 2 _test.go files and exactly ONE deadlocks, by its own design -- the semantic remedy (a package init that does not hold the type-initializer lock while it runs) is a converter design question recorded on the board with a population of one, not built ahead of a second case. Withdrawn from BOTH sides by the one --skip/-skip regexp and COUNTED IN DISCLOSED. Retires if a second case ever moves the design.

disclosures.name: TestEmptySlice
disclosures.reason: host-fatal HANG member, class REPRESENTATIONAL (coordinator ruling 2026-09-07 admitting the adjChunks pair; the class FIELD ratified to host-fatal at the same ruling once the schema was read at testConversion.go -- only host-fatal reaches hostFatalSkipExpression and only host-fatal may carry an empty signature, and a hanging test has no failure text to pin, so any other class is either refused at load or needs an invented signature that can never match). The test's FIRST statement is adjChunks() (mfinal_test.go:149, called at :168), an unbounded for{} that allocates *objtype -- objtype is [320]byte, reference-free -- until two live objects sit at exactly adjacent addresses, uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(c)) + 320 == uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(d)). SetFinalizer, runtime.GC and the <-fin receive below it are therefore NEVER REACHED: despite its file this is not a finalizer row, and the finalizer-deadlock reading of it was retracted in full once the spin was measured. Solo at a 5 m deadline the host burns 0.99 cores sustained across 255 s with the working set growing 125.4 -> 157.7 MB and emits no terminal action, against Go passing the same test in the same comparison (i9). MEASURED on both sides. Native Go at the pinned go1.23.12 finds the pair at ITERATION 2, minimum delta exactly 320 over 191 of 197 consecutive gaps, because Go's size class for a 320-byte object IS 320 and Go stores no per-object header. The CONVERTED path has a hard floor of 344 with ZERO hits at 320 across 199,999 pairs (i9, mailbox d0687ff2), and 344 is independently DERIVED from the CoreCLR x64 object layout as 8 sync block + 8 method-table pointer + 8 length and padding + 320 payload. Two distinct non-overlapping objects are separated by at least the size of the first, so 320 is below the smallest gap this object model CAN produce and the search cannot terminate. REPRESENTATIONAL rather than unimplemented: the assertion references the FOREIGN system's own heap layout, which a correct port answers differently by construction; the row's other verdicts are exactly what an unbuilt implementation would satisfy, so this is NOT an E3 row exclusion and the row stays in the denominator. Withdrawn from BOTH sides by the one --skip/-skip regexp and COUNTED IN DISCLOSED. RETIRES when a 320-byte Go allocation has a 320-byte managed footprint.

disclosures.name: TestCrashWhileTracing
disclosures.reason: host-fatal CRASH member (coordinator ruling 2026-09-07). A crash produces no row to pin, so this is the skip-list kind rather than a disclosure of a failing verdict. FACT ABOUT TODAY'S HOST: the test binary dies on an unrecovered panic in a goroutine at this row -- index 104 of 883 in file order -- and the death SHADOWS every later test, leaving 799 rows UNMEASURED; excluding this row alone raised terminal verdicts from 84 to 104 (i9, measured, ungated vs gated at master 5a27a8972). ROOTED end to end and the root is NOT a host defect: runtime.StartTrace is hand-owned on linux and windows and refuses by name because the CLR has no per-thread g (runtime/<goos>/trace_impl.cs), runtime/trace.Start early-returns on that error BEFORE spawning its writer goroutine so nothing is ever written to the child's stdout, the parent's traceparse.NewReader then fails version.ReadHeader's Fscanf on the "go 1." literal, and t.Fatalf aborts the test BEFORE cmd.Wait(); testenv's t.Cleanup cancels the context, os/exec's watchCtx -- still parked because Wait never drained resultc -- takes ctx.Done() and calls cmd.Cancel, whose else branch t.Logf's after the test has completed, and Go's own testing panics on a post-completion log. Every step from the Fatalf onward is FAITHFUL GO (internal/testenv/exec.go:199 and :205, os/exec/exec.go:772); Go never reaches the failing header read because Go's tracer works. The entry is the UNBLOCK, not the answer: it turns 799 unmeasured rows into measurable ones in one cut, and the tracer capability itself remains open work rather than a settled frontier. RETIRES when the test re-admitted produces a terminal verdict. AMENDMENT 2026-09-13 (C1) -- THE 1-6/7-8 MARKING, ruled at f5b35f351 as one dated amendment to be written only once i9's item-4 tail was in. LINKS 1-6 OF THE CHAIN ABOVE ARE READ: source-read at named lines on both sides (runtime/<goos>/trace_impl.cs, runtime/trace/trace.cs, internal/trace/reader.go, crash_test.go). LINKS 7-8 -- testenv's t.Cleanup cancel reaching os/exec's parked watchCtx, and the cmd.Cancel else-branch t.Logf that Go's own testing panics on -- were marked CONSEQUENCE-NOT-MEASURED: a reading of the code's own consequence, not a run. THE TAIL IS IN AND IT DOES NOT MEASURE THEM AT THIS ROW: i9 0dd133719 on landed master 44f858717 (Release, tiered false, .NET 10.0.11, rc=1, 169 s) reaches 185 of 880 verdicts with 695 never reached, and this row is not among them. NOR CAN ANY RUN MEASURE THEM HERE, IN EITHER CONFIGURATION, AND THAT IS THE FINDING RATHER THAN A GAP: run SOLO, the row's cleanup fires while the test is still live, so the late log cannot happen -- measured 2026-09-06, the row fails cleanly in 2.33 s and the host lives (src/tests/GolibTests/LogAfterCompleteTests.cs:34-39, which names this row as the WRONG instrument for exactly this reason); run FULL, this entry's own name enters hostFatalSkipExpression's regexp (src/go2cs/testConversion.go:6600) and withdraws the row from both sides. The entry forecloses its own confirming measurement. WHAT IS MEASURED is links 7-8's TERMINAL SHAPE, at the next door rather than this one: TestLockOSThreadNesting dies on "panic: Log in goroutine after TestLockOSThreadNesting has completed", thrown at src/core/testing/TestExecution.cs:418 after the ancestor walk at :407 finds no live ancestor (root-read by C1 at 18a34299f; the walk is Go's logDepth shape, landed 1aff2a352 and an ancestor of the tail's own tree) -- the same post-completion-log kill links 7-8 describe, and faithful, since Go panics on that condition too. SO THE MARKING STANDS AS: 1-6 READ; 7-8 READ AND MECHANISM-CONFIRMED AT A SIBLING DOOR, NEVER MEASURED AT THIS ROW, AND NOT MEASURABLE AT IT. Nothing above this amendment changes, the RETIRES trigger included. AMENDED 2026-09-28 (TRAIN I fixup, merge-hazard review): the ROOT above is STALE. Since the managed tracer (Q28) StartTrace starts golib's ExecutionTracer and runtime/trace.Start spawns its writer goroutine, and since TRAIN I seat 6 that is true on all three targets, with the start inside the stop-the-world pair. What remains open, unmeasured: whether the header queued at Start reaches the child's stdout before the child's init panic, and user-log events, which are never emitted. The entry stays host-fatal until a probe runs the row with the exclusion lifted and reads it (queued after TRAIN I lands).

disclosures.name: TestSetPanicOnFault
disclosures.reason: host-fatal CRASH member (coordinator ruling 2026-09-26, the P1 host-fatal seat). runtime_test.go sets debug.SetPanicOnFault(true) and then reads one byte through (*byte)(unsafe.Pointer(addr)) for each of the 19 faultAddrs (0, 1, 0xfff and 16 high kernel or malformed addresses), recovering each fault as a panic and failing only if none faulted. Go turns the SIGSEGV into a recoverable panic; the CLR does not. MEASURED on linux (P1, the stack 959a88df3 plus the metrics-histogram fix 0a074655e, Release, tiered off): the host dies with "Fatal error. System.AccessViolationException: Attempted to read or write protected memory" at ж<byte>.op_OnesComplement inside testSetPanicOnFault, no verdict is written, and every later test in the phase is lost. .NET treats an access violation as a corrupted-state fault that managed code cannot catch, so there is no managed refusal to prefer over a skip here: the fault happens inside the read, not in any runtime function that could refuse first. Which of the addresses faulted first is NOT measured (the test logs an address only after a read succeeds). Windows and darwin are NOT measured; the entry carries no platforms field because the uncatchable access violation is a property of the CLR on every target, which is inferred, not read. runtime/debug's TestPanicOnFault is the same fault class and the first member of this class. Withdrawn from BOTH sides by the one --skip/-skip regexp and COUNTED IN DISCLOSED. RETIRES when the managed runtime can recover a hardware fault as a panic.

disclosures.name: TestUserArenaLiveness/Free
disclosures.signature: expected arena-referenced object to be finalized
disclosures.reason: the test gives an arena object v a pointer to a heap object with a finalizer, drops v (`v = nil`), frees the arena (or, in /Finalizer, drops it), and then requires that finalizer to run, from inside the same still-running frame. Go's per-safepoint liveness maps drop v at its last use; the CLR reports the slots of a frame with exception handling (the converted defer's try/finally) live for the frame's whole lifetime, so v and everything it references stay rooted while the test is looking. The arena itself releases everything it allocated (arena_impl.cs, C2 C3 USER ARENAS). Measured on linux, Release, tiered off, as a one-axis A/B over the frame alone: the identical sequence (allocate smallPointerMix through UserArena.New, set its C to a fresh heap object, SetFinalizer on it, Free, runtime.GC() twice) run behind a RETURNED NoInlining call leaves v, v.C and the arena all collected (weak references dead), while inline in the test frame v and v.C stay alive even with the test's `x` and `v` explicitly cleared and v held past the clearing store. GolibTests' RuntimeUserArenaTests.AnObjectReachableOnlyFromTheArenaLivesUntilFree guards the arena half. The same class as runtime/debug's TestFreeOSMemory. RETIRES when the host reports frame liveness per safepoint, or the converter can end a local's lifetime at its last use.

disclosures.name: TestUserArenaLiveness/Finalizer
disclosures.signature: expected arena-referenced object to be finalized
disclosures.reason: Same frame-liveness retention as TestUserArenaLiveness/Free, with the arena dropped instead of freed (its handle unreachable after `arena = nil`): the arena and its allocation list are collected, and v, still reported live by the test frame, keeps the finalizer's object alive. Measured in the same A/B as /Free.

disclosures.name: TestReadMetrics
disclosures.reason: deferred (OQ-4, ruled 2026-09-28): /gc/heap/live:bytes reads gcController.heapMarked, which Go writes at mark termination (gcMarkTermination -> gcController.resetLive); the managed host runs no Go mark phase, so it reads 0. The line is NOT separable from Go's heap accounting: the test bounds live <= MemStats.HeapSys, and ReadMetricsSlow's MemStats come from Go's own readmemstats_m, whose HeapSys = gcController.heapInUse + heapFree + heapReleased, also 0 here, so writing heapMarked alone turns this line into 'live bytes: N > heap sys: 0'. Feeding HeapSys means feeding the heap accounting COHERENTLY: runtime's test binary enables doubleCheckReadMemStats (gc_test.go's init), and readmemstats_m then throws inside the stopped world -- host-fatal -- unless heapInUse, heapReleased, the retained heap, totalAlloc, totalFree and mappedReady all agree with consistentHeapStats.read, whose hand-own returns the zero delta. TestReadMetrics' gogc and gomemlimit lines match Go since M1 (claude/c1-gcpacer-knobs 5dd6bce97b); a failure without this line is a mismatch.
disclosures.want: 0 < /gc/heap/live:bytes <= MemStats.HeapSys, the MemStats ReadMetricsSlow reads through readmemstats_m in the same stopped world
disclosures.reading: 0 on linux/amd64 at 5dd6bce97b, Release (the go2cs -tests runtime row filtered to TestReadMetrics): gcController.heapMarked = 0 and HeapSys = 0; the test printed only 'live bytes is 0' (at 3d3883d4bb, before M1, it also printed the gogc and gomemlimit lines)

halves.signature: found no time spent on GC work
halves.reason: runtime-capability (ruled 2026-09-27 00:35, not reopened 2026-09-28, ledger 96edeb700a): Go's linux-only check wants some GC mark CPU time in /cpu/classes/gc/mark/{assist,dedicated,idle}. The managed host's collections are the CLR's, and a blocking CLR collection marks INSIDE its pause, so Go's own accounting puts that time in /cpu/classes/gc/pause (non-zero here) and the three mark classes stay 0; a background CLR gen2's mark time is not separately measurable, and runtime.GC() is a blocking Collect, so even a background-GC measure would read 0 for this test. Scoped to linux because Go's source makes the check only there (runtime.GOOS == "linux"). The rest of the test's CPU identities hold (gc/total = the four gc classes, total = gc + scavenge + user + idle).

structural (ruled 2026-09-28, ledger 96edeb700a): /gc/scan/{heap,stack,globals}:bytes read gcController.heapScan, lastStackScan and globalsScan, which Go writes at mark termination from its own pointer bitmaps. The CLR does not separate scannable bytes from pointer-free ones, so no managed measurement means the same quantity, and the honest reading is 0 (DESIGN-readmemstats-surface's rule: a field is answered only when a managed measurement means what the Go field means). Every target: the check is unconditional.

disclosures.name: TestStartLine/inline
disclosures.signature: caller runtime_test.inlineFunc1 inlined got false want true
disclosures.reason: runtime-capability (census A2, COORD ruling 2026-09-28, B2's class): the subtest asserts that Go's COMPILER inlined inlineFunc1 into inlineFunc, reading it as runtime.Frame.Func == nil (Go leaves Func nil only for an inlined frame), before it reads the start line. go2cs keeps Go's function boundaries one-for-one, the project's chosen design, so no function is ever inlined and every Go frame carries its function's interned *Func (runtime Frames.Next, D3). The frame is therefore reported NOT inlined, which is true of this host, and the subtest panics at its own inlining check. Faking a nil Func for functions Go would have inlined would report a compiler decision this host never made. Pinned to that panic text alone: the same subtest's start-line half is measured by its non-inlined siblings (normal, multiline-declaration, blank-lines, normal-closure), which pass, so any other failure here is a real defect, not this disclosure. Retires only if go2cs ever inlines a Go function.

disclosures.name: TestLineNumber
disclosures.reason: structural (census A2 D1b, OWNER RULING 2026-09-28 via COORD: disclose, no emission change). The test reads runtime.Caller's line for calls placed on DIFFERENT lines of ONE statement or one package var spec: composite-literal elements (compLit, arrayLit, sliceLit), map keys and values (mapLit), the operands of a multi-line sum (intLit) and the arguments of a multi-line call (l39, l40). The proof, for the C# the converter emits: .NET line data is a SEQUENCE POINT per statement or field initializer, and a frame's line is the sequence point at or before its IL offset, so every call inside one statement reports that statement's first line; no marker the converter writes can put two lines inside one sequence point. The single-line half (firstLine, lineVar1, lineVar2a, lineVar2b, arrayLit[0], sliceLit[0], l38) is D1a's and passes where D1a's package-var position markers are present (claude/i9-line-markers 6d69f68782); this entry is PINNED TO THAT POST-D1a TEXT, whose first failing line is compLit[0].lineA at firstLine+5 (the spec's own line), so it admits the row only where D1a holds and a D1a regression reads as a mismatch, never as this disclosure. Named, unscheduled retirement plan (the owner's): extra PDB sequence points written in the BUILD at each such call, never in the emitted C#.
